claim: Mutations of SMC5/6 components cause developmental defects, including primary microcephaly.
source: Mutations of SMC5/6 components cause developmental defects, including primary microcephaly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Smc5 cKO mice exhibited neurodevelopmental defects due to neural progenitor cell (NPC) apoptosis.
source: Smc5 cKO mice exhibited neurodevelopmental defects due to neural progenitor cell (NPC) apoptosis, which led to reduction in cortical layer neurons.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: Smc5 cKO NPCs formed DNA bridges during mitosis and underwent chromosome missegregation.
source: Smc5 cKO NPCs formed DNA bridges during mitosis and underwent chromosome missegregation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1H-I showing abnormal mitotic cells.

claim: SMC5/6 depletion triggers a CHEK2-p53 DNA damage response.
source: SMC5/6 depletion triggers a CHEK2-p53 DNA damage response, as concomitant deletion of the Trp53 tumor suppressor or Chek2 DNA damage checkpoint kinase rescued Smc5 cKO neurodevelopmental defects.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by rescue experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Absence of SMC5/6 leads to DNA replication stress at late-replicating regions such as pericentromeric heterochromatin.
source: Further assessment using Smc5 cKO and auxin-inducible degron systems demonstrated that absence of SMC5/6 leads to DNA replication stress at late-replicating regions such as pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 4 and 6 showing FANCD2 accumulation and MiDAS at pericentromeric regions.

claim: SMC5/6 is important for completion of DNA replication prior to entering mitosis.
source: In summary, SMC5/6 is important for completion of DNA replication prior to entering mitosis, which ensures accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary conclusion and supported by DNA fiber assays and MiDAS data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: SMC5/6 functions are critical in highly proliferative stem cells during organism development.
source: Thus, SMC5/6 functions are critical in highly proliferative stem cells during organism development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion based on the findings in NPCs and mESCs.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex is composed of a heterodimer of SMC5 and SMC6, which interact at their central hinge domains.
source: The SMC5/6 complex is composed of a heterodimer of SMC5 and SMC6, which interact at their central hinge domains.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about SMC5/6 structure.

claim: SMC5 and SMC6 harbor long coiled coil domains emanating from both sides of the hinge domain that fold back on each other to form an ATPase at the juxtaposed C and N termini.
source: SMC5 and SMC6 harbor long coiled coil domains emanating from both sides of the hinge domain that fold back on each other to form an ATPase at the juxtaposed C and N termini (Hassler et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Hassler et al., 2018.

claim: The ATPase head/tail domains of SMC5 and SMC6 are bridged by NSMCE4A, a kleisin protein.
source: The ATPase head/tail domains of SMC5 and SMC6 are bridged by NSMCE4A (non-SMC element 4A), a kleisin protein.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about SMC5/6 structure.

claim: NSMCE4A interacts with NSMCE1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and NSMCE3, a MAGE domain-containing protein.
source: NSMCE4A interacts with NSMCE1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and NSMCE3, a MAGE (melanoma-associated antigen gene) domain-containing protein (Palecek et al., 2006; Pebernard et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Palecek et al., 2006 and Pebernard et al., 2008a.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex comprises an E3 SUMO ligase, NSMCE2, which interacts with a region of the coiled coil domain of SMC5.
source: Additionally, the SMC5/6 complex comprises an E3 SUMO ligase, NSMCE2, which interacts with a region of the coiled coil domain of SMC5 (Andrews et al., 2005; Zhao and Blobel, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Andrews et al., 2005 and Zhao and Blobel, 2005.

claim: SLF1 and SLF2 form a dimer that primarily interacts with the SMC5/6 complex during DNA repair in response to DNA lesions that block DNA replication.
source: Two additional proteins, SLF1 and SLF2 (SMC5/6 localization factors), form a dimer that primarily interacts with the SMC5/6 complex during DNA repair in response to DNA lesions that block DNA replication (Räschle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Räschle et al., 2015.

claim: SLF2 binds to the arms of SMC5 and SMC6 and may lock the arms together to immobilize SMC5/6 at sites of DNA damage.
source: SLF2 binds to the arms of SMC5 and SMC6 and may lock the arms together to immobilize SMC5/6 at sites of DNA damage (Adamus et al., 2020; Räschle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Adamus et al., 2020 and Räschle et al., 2015.

claim: Mutations in cohesin components lead to an array of abnormalities, including growth retardation and cognitive impairment.
source: Collectively known as cohesinopathies, mutations in cohesin components lead to an array of abnormalities, including growth retardation and cognitive impairment (Boyle et al., 2015; Piché et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Boyle et al., 2015 and Piché et al., 2019.

claim: Mutations in condensin components lead to primary microcephaly due to chromosome decatenation failure during mitosis.
source: Mutations in condensin components lead to primary microcephaly due to chromosome decatenation failure during mitosis (Martin et al., 2016; Nishide and Hirano, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Martin et al., 2016 and Nishide and Hirano, 2014.

claim: Mutations in NSMCE3 result in immunodeficiency and lung disease, where patient-derived cells exhibit hallmarks of chromosome instability and replication stress.
source: In regard to SMC5/6, mutations in NSMCE3 result in immunodeficiency and lung disease, where patient-derived cells exhibit hallmarks of chromosome instability and replication stress (van der Crabben et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to van der Crabben et al., 2016.

claim: Mutation of NSMCE2 causes primordial dwarfism and primary congenital microcephaly.
source: Moreover, mutation of NSMCE2 causes primordial dwarfism and primary congenital microcephaly (Payne et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Payne et al., 2014.

claim: Patient cells harboring the NSMCE2 mutation revealed chromosome instability and increased sensitivity to DNA replication stress.
source: Assessment of patient cells harboring the NSMCE2 mutation revealed chromosome instability and increased sensitivity to DNA replication stress (Payne et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Payne et al., 2014.

claim: Genetic variations in SMC5 are potentially associated with congenital defects including heart and neurodevelopmental anomalies.
source: Furthermore, genetic variations in other components of the SMC5/6 complex, including SMC5, are potentially associated with congenital defects including heart and neurodevelopmental anomalies (Homsy et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2017; Landrum et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Homsy et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2017; and Landrum et al., 2018.

claim: Conditional knockout of Nsmce2 in mice during adulthood causes premature aging and susceptibility to cancer.
source: One study found that conditional knockout (cKO) of Nsmce2 in mice during adulthood causes premature aging and susceptibility to cancer (Jacome et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Jacome et al., 2015.

claim: Cell cultures from mice with Nsmce2 mutation revealed increased formation of micronuclei and sister chromatid exchange events.
source: Analysis of cell cultures from mice with Nsmce2 mutation revealed increased formation of micronuclei and sister chromatid exchange events (Jacome et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Jacome et al., 2015.

claim: SMC5/6 is largely dispensable for spermatogenesis but is essential for mediating chromosome segregation during oogenesis.
source: Two other studies have focused on using Smc5 cKO to address the sexually dimorphic roles of SMC5/6 during gametogenesis, wherein SMC5/6 is largely dispensable for spermatogenesis but is essential for mediating chromosome segregation during oogenesis (Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hwang et al., 2018 and Hwang et al., 2017.

claim: Null mutations of SMC5/6 components in mice result in a failure to reach blastocyst stage.
source: Null mutations of SMC5/6 components in mice result in a failure to reach blastocyst stage (Hwang et al., 2017; Jacome et al., 2015; Ju et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hwang et al., 2017; Jacome et al., 2015; and Ju et al., 2013.

claim: NPCs reside in the ventricular zone (VZ) of the cerebral cortex and undergo symmetric and asymmetric divisions to self-renew and produce intermediate progenitors (IPs) or neurons.
source: NPCs reside in the ventricular zone (VZ) of the cerebral cortex and undergo symmetric and asymmetric divisions to self-renew and produce intermediate progenitors (IPs) or neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge about cortical development.

claim: IPs are mainly located in the subventricular zone (SVZ).
source: IPs are mainly located in the subventricular zone (SVZ) (Kowalczyk et al., 2009; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Kowalczyk et al., 2009 and Paridaen and Huttner, 2014.

claim: Early-born neurons give rise to deep cortical layers (V and VI) and late-born neurons form superficial layers (II–IV).
source: This migration occurs in an inside-out manner, in which early-born neurons give rise to deep cortical layers (V and VI) and late-born neurons form superficial layers (II–IV) (Molyneaux et al., 2007; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; Shibata et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Molyneaux et al., 2007; Paridaen and Huttner, 2014; and Shibata et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of NPC genomic integrity during embryonic development causes increased NPC apoptosis, reduced neuron production, and neuron mislocalization, ultimately resulting in decreased cortex size or microcephaly.
source: Disruption of NPC genomic integrity during embryonic development causes increased NPC apoptosis, reduced neuron production, and neuron mislocalization, ultimately resulting in decreased cortex size or microcephaly (McKinnon, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to McKinnon, 2013.

claim: The rapid proliferative activity of NPCs imparts a high degree of endogenous replication stress and DNA damage.
source: The rapid proliferative activity of NPCs imparts a high degree of endogenous replication stress and DNA damage, which can lead to the formation of excess single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-strand breaks (DSBs) (Harley et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012; McKinnon, 2017; O'Driscoll, 2017; Reynolds et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Harley et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2012; McKinnon, 2017; O'Driscoll, 2017; and Reynolds et al., 2017.

claim: ATM and ATR kinases play independent and essential roles in DDR, and their loss can lead to neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration.
source: ATM and ATR kinases play independent and essential roles in DDR, and their loss can lead to neurodevelopmental disorders and neurodegeneration (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017; Madabhushi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017 and Madabhushi et al., 2014.

claim: ATM can be activated by DSBs in both NPCs and immature neurons, while ATR is responsible for G2/M checkpoint induced by RPA-bound ssDNA during replication stress in proliferating NPCs.
source: ATM can be activated by DSBs in both NPCs and immature neurons, while ATR is responsible for G2/M checkpoint induced by RPA-bound ssDNA during replication stress in proliferating NPCs (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017.

claim: DNA DSB repair by homology-directed repair (HDR) is prevalent in mitotically active NPCs, and non-homologous end joining becomes the pathway for DNA repair in postmitotic neurons.
source: DNA DSB repair by homology-directed repair (HDR) is prevalent in mitotically active NPCs, and non-homologous end joining becomes the pathway for DNA repair in postmitotic neurons (Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017; Madabhushi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Enriquez-Rios et al., 2017 and Madabhushi et al., 2014.

claim: ATR and ATM act through their respective downstream targets CHEK1 and CHEK2 to activate p53-mediated cell cycle arrest or apoptosis if DNA damage remains unrepaired.
source: ATR and ATM act through their respective downstream targets CHEK1 and CHEK2 to activate p53-mediated cell cycle arrest or apoptosis if DNA damage remains unrepaired (Sengupta and Harris, 2005; Shaltiel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Sengupta and Harris, 2005 and Shaltiel et al., 2015.

claim: Depletion of SMC5 at early stages of mouse brain development resulted in reduced cerebral cortex size due to mitotic abnormalities in NPCs, perturbed differentiation, and increased apoptosis.
source: In this study, we show that depletion of SMC5 at early stages of mouse brain development resulted in reduced cerebral cortex size due to mitotic abnormalities in NPCs, perturbed differentiation, and increased apoptosis, which collectively affected cortical layer formation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a summary of the study's findings and is supported by data in Figures 1-3.

claim: SMC5 depletion leads to genome instability and DDR activation.
source: We observed that SMC5 depletion leads to genome instability and DDR activation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: The cortex size of Smc5 cKO mice was restored upon knockout of Trp53 or Chek2 genes.
source: We found that the cortex size of Smc5 cKO mice was restored upon knockout of Trp53 or Chek2 genes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: SMC5/6 is important for DNA replication fork stability.
source: Subsequently, using an auxin-inducible degron (AID) system to deplete SMC5 in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs) we mimicked cell proliferation and cell death phenotypes observed in vivo, which were also rescued by inhibition of p53 or CHEK2. Using the AID system, we determined that SMC5/6 is important for DNA replication fork stability and propose a role for SMC5/6 in the processing of under-replicated DNA intermediates to ensure accurate chromosome segregation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5.

claim: Exon 4 of the Smc5 cKO allele was flanked by loxP Cre recombinase target sequences.
source: Exon 4 of the Smc5 cKO allele was flanked by loxP Cre recombinase target sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Depletion of SMC5 via Smc5 cKO has been shown to destabilize the entire SMC5/6 complex.
source: Depletion of SMC5 via Smc5 cKO has been shown to destabilize the entire SMC5/6 complex (Gaddipati et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to previous studies.

claim: Nestin-Cre is expressed throughout the central nervous system.
source: Nestin-Cre is expressed throughout the central nervous system (Dubois et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Dubois et al., 2006.

claim: Emx1-Cre expression is restricted to the mouse cerebral cortex.
source: Emx1-Cre expression is restricted to the mouse cerebral cortex (Gorski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: Nestin-Cre and Emx1-Cre recombinases demonstrate robust expression in the mouse cortex at E12.5.
source: Nestin-Cre and Emx1-Cre recombinases demonstrate robust expression in the mouse cortex at E12.5, and the use of either one to mediate Smc5 cKO was expected to result in a similar phenotype during cortex development (Insolera et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Insolera et al., 2014.

claim: The protein levels of SMC5 and SMC6 were only partially diminished in E13.5 brains.
source: Although we observed conditional mutation of Smc5 in E13.5 brains, the protein levels of SMC5 and SMC6 were only partially diminished (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The deletion in Smc5 was accompanied by a substantial reduction in SMC5 and SMC6 protein levels in E16.5 embryos.
source: In contrast, the deletion in Smc5 was accompanied by a substantial reduction in SMC5 and SMC6 protein levels in E16.5 embryos (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: Some degree of DNA excision was also observed in kidneys and muscles in Smc5 cKO samples.
source: Since Nestin is expressed in progenitor cells of tissues other than neural, some degree of DNA excision was also observed in kidneys and muscles in our samples (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Bernal and Arranz, 2018; Sakairi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, with citations to Bernal and Arranz, 2018 and Sakairi et al., 2007.

claim: SMC5 depletion in the developing mouse cortex resulted in a significant increase in cleaved caspase 3 (CASP3)-positive cells in Smc5 cKO compared to controls in both E13.5 and E16.5 cortices.
source: SMC5 depletion in the developing mouse cortex resulted in a significant increase in cleaved caspase 3 (CASP3)-positive cells in Smc5 cKO compared to controls in both E13.5 and E16.5 cortices (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: The increase in the number of cells undergoing apoptotic DNA fragmentation was most pronounced in E16.5 cortices.
source: The increase in the number of cells undergoing apoptotic DNA fragmentation was most pronounced in E16.5 cortices (Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1F,G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: The depletion of SMC5 in mESCs causes chromosome segregation defects during mitosis.
source: We have previously shown that the depletion of SMC5 in mESCs causes chromosome segregation defects during mitosis (Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Hwang et al., 2017 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claim: The percentage of NPCs undergoing abnormal mitosis with characteristic DNA bridges and lagging chromosomes at anaphase was elevated in Smc5 cKO compared to control.
source: The percentage of NPCs undergoing abnormal mitosis with characteristic DNA bridges and lagging chromosomes at anaphase was elevated in Smc5 cKO compared to control (Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: There was an increase in abnormal anaphase cells when comparing Smc5 cKO cortices from E13.5 to E16.5 (9% versus 38%, respectively).
source: We observed an increase in abnormal anaphase cells when comparing Smc5 cKO cortices from E13.5 to E16.5 (9% versus 38%, respectively; Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Depletion of SMC5 in NPCs caused a significant increase in the number of anaphase cells with oblique division axis (<60°).
source: Depletion of SMC5 in NPCs caused a significant increase in the number of anaphase cells with oblique division axis (<60°) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Tissue-specific depletion of SMC5 did not affect overall embryonic development and mice survived to adulthood without additional morphological abnormalities.
source: Tissue-specific depletion of SMC5 did not affect overall embryonic development and mice survived to adulthood without additional morphological abnormalities.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations of the mice.

claim: The difference in brain weight and cortex size in Smc5 cKO mediated by Nestin-Cre was significant at postnatal day 0/1 (P0/1) and became more prominent in adults (P55).
source: The difference in brain weight and cortex size in Smc5 cKO mediated by Nestin-Cre was significant at postnatal day 0/1 (P0/1) and became more prominent in adults (P55) (Figure 1J–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1J–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Emx1-Cre-mediated Smc5 cKO also led to reduced brain weight and cortex size in newborn and adult mice compared to littermate controls.
source: Emx1-Cre-mediated Smc5 cKO also led to reduced brain weight and cortex size in newborn and adult mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 1N,O and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1N,O and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–L.

claim: A significant delay in the time taken to contact the adhesive in Smc5 cKO mice compared to control mice was observed, which is evidence of impaired sensory activity.
source: We observed a significant delay in the time taken to contact the adhesive in Smc5 cKO mice compared to control mice, which is evidence of impaired sensory activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Smc5 cKO mice underperformed in the inverted screen test compared to control mice.
source: Smc5 cKO mice underperformed in this test compared to control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Smc5 cKO mice displayed less forelimb use during vertical exploration compared to controls.
source: Smc5 cKO mice displayed less forelimb use during vertical exploration compared to controls, as demonstrated by the elevated ratio of rears with no paws touching the cylinder wall and the reduced ratio of rears with two paws touching the cylinder wall (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: The reduced cortex size mediated by SMC5 depletion results in impaired sensorimotor function in mice.
source: Collectively, these behavioral tests revealed that the reduced cortex size mediated by SMC5 depletion results in impaired sensorimotor function in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the behavioral tests.

claim: Aged adult (P293/295) Smc5 cKO brains showed reduced cortex size and thickness, as well as decreased brain weight, compared to the control mice.
source: Following conclusion of the sensorimotor assays, the aged adult (P293/295) Smc5 cKO brains were assessed and showed reduced cortex size and thickness, as well as decreased brain weight, compared to the control mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E–H.

claim: Smc5 cKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) accumulate RAD51 foci in the presence of replicative stress.
source: We previously showed that Smc5 cKO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) accumulate RAD51 foci in the presence of replicative stress (Gaddipati et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to Gaddipati et al., 2019.

claim: Analysis of E16.5 embryonic tissues revealed upregulation of RAD51 in the neural cortex of Smc5 cKO mice.
source: Analysis of E16.5 embryonic tissues revealed upregulation of RAD51 in the neural cortex of Smc5 cKO mice (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: p53 is upregulated and activated in MEFs and mESCs following Smc5 cKO.
source: We have previously demonstrated that p53 is upregulated and activated in MEFs and mESCs following Smc5 cKO (Gaddipati et al., 2019; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Gaddipati et al., 2019 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claim: p53 activation is observed in the progenitor zone of E16.5 Smc5 cKO cortices.
source: Similarly, we observe p53 activation in the progenitor zone of E16.5 Smc5 cKO cortices (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Brain weight was not affected in mice that were Trp53 KO alone.
source: Brain weight was not affected in mice that were Trp53 KO alone (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The brain weight, cortex area, and cortical thickness size of Smc5, Trp53 double knockout (dKO) adult mice were comparable to littermate controls.
source: The analysis of Smc5, Trp53 double knockout (dKO) adult mice revealed that the brain weight, cortex area, and cortical thickness size were comparable to littermate controls (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Significant differences were observed between Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5 cKO mouse brain parameters.
source: However, significant differences were observed compared to Smc5 cKO mouse brain parameters (Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Smc5 cKO in the mouse brain causes a p53-dependent apoptosis of neural cells.
source: These data confirm that Smc5 cKO in the mouse brain causes a p53-dependent apoptosis of neural cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the rescue experiments.

claim: Adult Smc5, Chek2 dKO mouse brain weight, cortical thickness, and cortex area were significantly larger than Smc5 cKO mice.
source: Indeed, adult Smc5, Chek2 dKO mouse brain weight, cortical thickness, and cortex area were significantly larger than Smc5 cKO mice (Figure 2B–D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B–D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The brain weight and cortex area of Smc5, Chek2 dKO mice were not restored to levels equivalent to the control or Chek2 KO mice.
source: However, the brain weight and cortex area were not restored to levels equivalent to the control or Chek2 KO mice (Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B,D,F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Abrogation of SMC5/6 functions results in DNA damage induced by DSBs and p53-mediated apoptosis likely through the ATM-CHEK2-p53 DDR signaling pathway.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that abrogation of SMC5/6 functions results in DNA damage induced by DSBs and p53-mediated apoptosis likely through the ATM-CHEK2-p53 DDR signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: The brain weight and cortex size of Smc5, Trp53bp1 dKO adult mice were not restored.
source: Thus, we analyzed Smc5, Trp53bp1 dKO adult mice and revealed that the brain weight and cortex size were not restored (Figure 2D,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D,G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The loss of SMC5/6 complex functions induces a DDR independent of or epistatic with 53BP1-mediated signaling.
source: These results demonstrate that the loss of SMC5/6 complex functions induces a DDR independent of or epistatic with 53BP1-mediated signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the 53BP1 knockout experiments.

claim: Increased DNA fragmentation was not evident in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO P0/1 cortices.
source: In contrast to Smc5 cKO, increased DNA fragmentation was not evident in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO P0/1 cortices (Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Rescue of the cortex thickness defect caused by Smc5 cKO was observed when Trp53 or Chek2 are also mutated in P0/1 sagittal head cross-sections.
source: From analysis of P0/1 sagittal head cross-sections, we observed rescue of the cortex thickness defect caused by Smc5 cKO when Trp53 or Chek2 are also mutated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Depletion of SMC5 in the developing mouse cortex caused the displacement of apical NPCs marked by SOX2 and PAX6 into the area outside VZ.
source: Depletion of SMC5 in the developing mouse cortex caused the displacement of apical NPCs marked by SOX2 and PAX6 into the area outside VZ (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B; Englund et al., 2005; Ferri et al., 2004; Sansom et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, with citations to Englund et al., 2005; Ferri et al., 2004; and Sansom et al., 2009.

claim: The displacement tendency of apical NPCs was even more pronounced in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices.
source: This tendency was even more pronounced in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: An increase in the total number of SOX2+ and PAX6+ NPCs was observed in both Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO compared to the control.
source: Interestingly, we observed an increase in the total number of SOX2+ and PAX6+ NPCs in both Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO compared to the control (Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of TBR2+ IPs located in the SVZ of Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.
source: In contrast to apical NPCs, we observed a significant decrease in the number of TBR2+ IPs located in the SVZ of Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control (Figure 3G–I; Arnold et al., 2008; Englund et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G–I, with citations to Arnold et al., 2008 and Englund et al., 2005.

claim: The cortical area occupied by TBR2+ progenitors in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices was increased compared to the control.
source: The cortical area occupied by TBR2+ progenitors in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices was increased compared to the control (Figure 3G–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Smc5 cKO leads to ectopic localization of NPCs and significant loss of IPs.
source: These results demonstrate that Smc5 cKO leads to ectopic localization of NPCs and significant loss of IPs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the NPC and IP analysis.

claim: Mutation of Trp53 or Chek2 in conjunction with Smc5 cKO alleviates the loss of IPs but exacerbates NPC ectopic localization.
source: Mutation of Trp53 or Chek2 in conjunction with Smc5 cKO alleviates the loss of IPs but exacerbates NPC ectopic localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the double knockout analysis.

claim: A significant decrease in TBR1+ (layer VI), CTIP2+ (layer V), and SATB2+ (layers II–V) cells in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.
source: We observed a significant decrease in TBR1+ (layer VI), CTIP2+ (layer V), and SATB2+ (layers II–V) cells in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control (Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: The development of early- and late-born neuron populations were restored in Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices.
source: Assessment of the Smc5, Trp53 dKO and Smc5, Chek2 dKO cortices demonstrated that the development of early- and late-born neuron populations were restored (Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3J–O and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: SMC5 depletion causes abnormal positioning of apical NPCs and reduction in the populations of IPs, as well as deep and upper cortical layer neurons.
source: Taken together, SMC5 depletion causes abnormal positioning of apical NPCs and reduction in the populations of IPs, as well as deep and upper cortical layer neurons, suggesting a global impact on cortical development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary of the cortical development findings.

claim: Absence of p53 and CHEK2 prevents the loss of IPs and restores cortical layer-specific neuron numbers.
source: We also provide evidence that absence of p53 and CHEK2 prevents the loss of IPs and restores cortical layer-specific neuron numbers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the double knockout analysis.

claim: Smc5 cKO cortical sections had 20.2% less Ki67+ proliferating and 35.7% less H3P+ mitotic cells compared to control.
source: Smc5 cKO cortical sections had 20.2% less Ki67+ proliferating and 35.7% less H3P+ mitotic cells compared to control (Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: A 34.7% decrease in CldU+ populations in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control was observed.
source: We observed a 34.7% decrease in CldU+ populations in Smc5 cKO cortices compared to control (Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: There is an accumulation of cells in G1 phase of the cell cycle that are blocked from entering S phase in Smc5 cKO cortices.
source: The higher level of reduction in CldU+ and H3P+ populations compared to the reduction in total number of Ki67+ proliferating cells in Smc5 cKO cortices indicates that there is an accumulation of cells in G1 phase of the cell cycle that are blocked from entering S phase (Figure 4B,C,F,G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B,C,F,G.

claim: NPCs with extensive incorporation of CldU that were undergoing aberrant chromosome segregation were observed.
source: From our in vivo CldU pulse experiments, we observed NPCs with extensive incorporation of CldU that were undergoing aberrant chromosome segregation (Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Accumulation of two intensely stained H3P+ chromatin foci on both sides of the segregating chromosomes that also contained CldU was observed.
source: Further, we observed accumulation of two intensely stained H3P+ chromatin foci on both sides of the segregating chromosomes that also contained CldU (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: No CldU signal was observed between either of the two intensely stained H3P+ foci.
source: However, no CldU signal was observed between either of the two intensely stained H3P+ foci.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observations in Figure 4H.

claim: Increased number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO compared to control cells was observed, particularly at pericentromeric regions.
source: In addition, we observed increased number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO compared to control cells, particularly at pericentromeric regions (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4I–K.

claim: The number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO cells was increased by 6.5-fold compared to control.
source: The number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO cells was increased by 6.5-fold compared to control, while pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci were increased by 8.1-fold (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: Pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci were increased by 8.1-fold in Smc5 cKO cells compared to control.
source: The number of FANCD2+ foci in Smc5 cKO cells was increased by 6.5-fold compared to control, while pericentromeric FANCD2+ foci were increased by 8.1-fold (Figure 4J,K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: SMC5/6 components accumulate at pericentromeric heterochromatin regions of chromosomes.
source: We have previously shown that SMC5/6 components accumulate at pericentromeric heterochromatin regions of chromosomes (Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claim: A decrease in average width and intensity of pericentromeric H4K20 signal by 1.3- and 2.0-fold, respectively, in Smc5 cKO cells compared to control was observed.
source: Assessment of chromosome spreads prepared from control and Smc5 cKO E16.5 cortical cells revealed a decrease in average width and intensity of pericentromeric H4K20 signal by 1.3- and 2.0-fold, respectively, in Smc5 cKO cells compared to control (Figure 4L–N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4L–N and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The reduction in methylated pericentromeric H4K20 in Smc5 cKO cells may reflect under-replicated DNA and increased DNA damage.
source: Therefore, the reduction in methylated pericentromeric H4K20 in Smc5 cKO cells may reflect under-replicated DNA and increased DNA damage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the H4K20 methylation data.

claim: The reduction of SMC5 levels occurred as early as 30 min after IAA addition, with robust depletion occurring after 1 hr of IAA treatment.
source: We observed the reduction of SMC5 levels as early as 30 min after IAA addition, with robust depletion occurring after 1 hr of IAA treatment (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: IAA treatment triggered upregulation of acetyl-p53 (K379) and phospho-p53 (S389) by 2 hr and 48 hr, respectively.
source: Immunoblotting analysis showed that IAA treatment triggered upregulation of acetyl-p53 (K379) and phospho-p53 (S389) by 2 hr and 48 hr, respectively (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Smc5-AID mESCs undergo severe cell growth perturbations within 48 hr after SMC5 depletion.
source: This is consistent with the fact that Smc5-AID mESCs undergo severe cell growth perturbations within 48 hr after SMC5 depletion (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 38.2% of G1 phase cells, 26.2% of S/G2 phase cells, and 40.8% of prophase cells were positive for p-p53 in the IAA-treated group compared to 11.9%, 11.8%, and 7.0% of the control in respective stages.
source: Specifically, 38.2% of G1 phase cells, 26.2% of S/G2 phase cells, and 40.8% of prophase cells were positive for p-p53 in the IAA-treated group compared to 11.9%, 11.8%, and 7.0% of the control in respective stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The majority of p-p53+ cells were in G1 phase in the IAA-treated group, while the majority of p-p53+ cells in the control population were in S/G2 phase.
source: Further reaffirming this, the majority of p-p53+ cells were in G1 phase in the IAA-treated group, while the majority of p-p53+ cells in the control population were in S/G2 phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A 1.5-fold increase in the percentage of total G1 phase cells, a 1.5-fold decrease in the percentage of total S/G2 phase cells, and a 2.1-fold increase in the percentage of total prophase cells in the IAA-treated group compared to control was observed.
source: We also observed a 1.5-fold increase in the percentage of total G1 phase cells, a 1.5-fold decrease in the percentage of total S/G2 phase cells, and a 2.1-fold increase in the percentage of total prophase cells in the IAA-treated group compared to control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Concurrent treatment with IAA and CHEK2 inhibitor restored cell numbers similar to the CHEK2 inhibitor-only control.
source: Concurrent treatment with IAA and CHEK2 inhibitor restored cell numbers similar to the CHEK2 inhibitor-only control (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CHEK1 inhibition did not rescue cell growth defects after IAA treatment.
source: In contrast, CHEK1 inhibition did not rescue cell growth defects after IAA treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The main pathway triggering p53 activation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis upon SMC5 depletion in mESCs is CHEK2-mediated.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the main pathway triggering p53 activation, cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis upon SMC5 depletion in mESCs is CHEK2-mediated.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the inhibitor experiments.

claim: SMC5 depletion in CHEK2-inhibited mESCs resulted in 1.5-fold decrease in ongoing unidirectional forks compared to the inhibitor-only control.
source: We found that SMC5 depletion in CHEK2-inhibited mESCs resulted in 1.5-fold decrease in ongoing unidirectional forks compared to the inhibitor-only control (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Converging forks and stalled forks were increased by 1.6- and 2.2-fold, respectively, compared to control upon SMC5 depletion in CHEK2-inhibited mESCs.
source: In addition, converging forks and stalled forks were increased by 1.6- and 2.2-fold, respectively, compared to control (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G.

claim: A 1.3-fold reduced track length and 1.5-fold elevated CldU/IdU ratio in unidirectional dual-labeled forks upon SMC5 depletion with CHEK2 inhibition was observed.
source: We also observed 1.3-fold reduced track length and 1.5-fold elevated CldU/IdU ratio in unidirectional dual-labeled forks upon SMC5 depletion with CHEK2 inhibition (Figure 5I,J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5I,J.

claim: Higher frequency of MiDAS was observed in SMC5-depleted mESCs, indicated by EdU+ and dual EdU+FANCD2+ foci.
source: Higher frequency of MiDAS was observed in SMC5-depleted mESCs, indicated by EdU+ and dual EdU+FANCD2+ foci (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: The mean number of EdU+ and dual EdU+FANCD2+ foci per chromosome was increased by 3.6- and 4.3-fold, respectively, in SMC5-depleted mESCs compared to control.
source: The mean number of EdU+ and dual EdU+FANCD2+ foci per chromosome was increased by 3.6- and 4.3-fold, respectively, in SMC5-depleted mESCs compared to control (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Loss of SMC5 caused elevated MiDAS at pericentromeric regions, as indicated by dual EdU+CEN+ foci and triple EdU+FANCD2+CEN+ foci, which were increased by 4.7- and 6.2-fold, respectively.
source: Loss of SMC5 also caused elevated MiDAS at pericentromeric regions, as indicated by dual EdU+CEN+ foci and triple EdU+FANCD2+CEN+ foci, which were increased by 4.7- and 6.2-fold, respectively (Figure 6B,E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6B,E,F.

claim: The ratio of 'acrocentric' EdU foci to 'non-acrocentric' EdU foci was 1.47 and 1.91 in control and IAA-treated mESCs, respectively.
source: This ratio was 1.47 and 1.91 in control and IAA-treated mESCs, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The depletion of SMC5 in stem cells results in increased DNA replication stress.
source: Our data suggest that the depletion of SMC5 in stem cells results in increased DNA replication stress (Figure 5F-J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G-I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by DNA fiber assay data in Figure 5F-J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G-I.

claim: The major neurodevelopmental defects observed in Smc5 cKO model during embryogenesis were the displacement of apical NPCs into the cortical area outside the VZ and reduction in IPs and neurons of all cortical layers.
source: The major neurodevelopmental defects we observed in our Smc5 cKO model during embryogenesis were the displacement of apical NPCs into the cortical area outside the VZ and reduction in IPs and neurons of all cortical layers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: A proportion of NPCs in the Smc5 cKO cortex do not contribute to the development of IPs and fail to differentiate into layer-specific neurons.
source: Therefore, our data suggest that a proportion of NPCs in the Smc5 cKO cortex do not contribute to the development of IPs and fail to differentiate into layer-specific neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: cKO of Smc5 within the developing cortex does not affect animal survival into adulthood.
source: In contrast, cKO of Smc5 within the developing cortex does not affect animal survival into adulthood and can be used for longitudinal behavioral, sensorimotor, and neuronal activity analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on observations of the mice.

claim: Smc5 cKO during neurodevelopment did not result in accumulation of NPCs in S phase.
source: Smc5 cKO during neurodevelopment did not result in accumulation of NPCs in S phase, which indicated that the ATR-CHEK1 S phase checkpoint pathway did not trigger cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the cell cycle analysis.

claim: Smc5 cKO NPCs did not undergo mitotic delay.
source: Despite the chromosome segregation defects, Smc5 cKO NPCs did not undergo mitotic delay (Phan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Phan et al., 2020.

claim: p53- and CHEK2-mediated apoptosis were major drivers for the reduced cortex size following Smc5 cKO in NPCs.
source: We demonstrated that p53- and CHEK2-mediated apoptosis were major drivers for the reduced cortex size following Smc5 cKO in NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the genetic rescue experiments.

claim: The upregulation of acetyl-p53 at 2 hr after IAA treatment reveals that a DDR occurs nearly immediately upon SMC5 depletion.
source: Given that complete SMC5 depletion occurs only after 1–2 hr of IAA treatment, the upregulation of acetyl-p53 at this early time point reveals that a DDR occurs nearly immediately upon SMC5 depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the p53 activation kinetics.

claim: Previous studies in human cancer cells demonstrated an increase in unmodified p53 levels only within 2 days after SMC5/6 depletion by the AID system.
source: By contrast, previous studies in human cancer cells demonstrated an increase in unmodified p53 levels only within 2 days after SMC5/6 depletion by the AID system (Venegas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Venegas et al., 2020.

claim: The phosphorylation of p53 during prophase could be a consequence of late replication defects during G2 or the presence of under-replicated DNA.
source: As we observed perturbed replication in SMC5-depleted cells, it is conceivable that the phosphorylation of p53 during prophase could be a consequence of late replication defects during G2 or the presence of under-replicated DNA, while the accumulation of p-p53 during G1 phase may be caused by the inheritance of unresolved DNA damage by G1 daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculative interpretation of the p53 phosphorylation patterns.

claim: The accumulation of p-p53 during G1 phase may be caused by the inheritance of unresolved DNA damage by G1 daughter cells.
source: As we observed perturbed replication in SMC5-depleted cells, it is conceivable that the phosphorylation of p53 during prophase could be a consequence of late replication defects during G2 or the presence of under-replicated DNA, while the accumulation of p-p53 during G1 phase may be caused by the inheritance of unresolved DNA damage by G1 daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculative interpretation of the p53 phosphorylation patterns.

claim: Depletion of SMC5/6 components in human cancer cells (HCT116) or hTERT immortalized non-cancer cells (RPE1) caused activation of CHEK2 and stabilization of p53.
source: It was recently shown that depletion of SMC5/6 components in human cancer cells (HCT116) or hTERT immortalized non-cancer cells (RPE1) caused activation of CHEK2 and stabilization of p53 (Venegas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Venegas et al., 2020.

claim: Inactivation of TP53 did not alleviate the cell-cycle arrest, cell death, and senescence observed following SMC5/6 degradation in either HCT116 or RPE1 cells.
source: However, inactivation of TP53 did not alleviate the cell-cycle arrest, cell death, and senescence observed following SMC5/6 degradation in either HCT116 or RPE1 cells (Venegas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Venegas et al., 2020.

claim: An earlier study using human RPE1 cells showed slower progression of DNA replication upon RNAi-mediated depletion of SMC6.
source: Although an earlier study using human RPE1 cells showed slower progression of DNA replication upon RNAi-mediated depletion of SMC6, our previous work demonstrated timely entry and exit from S phase in SMC5-deficient mESCs (Gallego-Paez et al., 2014; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Gallego-Paez et al., 2014 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claim: Previous work demonstrated timely entry and exit from S phase in SMC5-deficient mESCs.
source: Although an earlier study using human RPE1 cells showed slower progression of DNA replication upon RNAi-mediated depletion of SMC6, our previous work demonstrated timely entry and exit from S phase in SMC5-deficient mESCs (Gallego-Paez et al., 2014; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Gallego-Paez et al., 2014 and Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016.

claim: DNA fiber studies in budding yeast have shown disrupted replication fork progression in Smc6 mutant cells under exogenous replication stress, but with no effects under unstressed conditions.
source: DNA fiber studies in budding yeast have shown disrupted replication fork progression in Smc6 mutant cells under exogenous replication stress, but with no effects under unstressed conditions (Bermúdez-López et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Bermúdez-López et al., 2010.

claim: A recent study using HCT116 cancer cells observed that the depletion of SMC5/6 complex components did not affect replication fork speed or CldU/IdU ratio.
source: In contrast to the results presented here, a recent study using HCT116 cancer cells observed that the depletion of SMC5/6 complex components did not affect replication fork speed or CldU/IdU ratio (Venegas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Venegas et al., 2020.

claim: mESCs and NPCs have higher levels of intrinsic replication stress due to their rapid rate of proliferation.
source: However, mESCs and NPCs have higher levels of intrinsic replication stress due to their rapid rate of proliferation (Ahuja et al., 2016; Arai et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2015; Waisman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Ahuja et al., 2016; Arai et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2015; and Waisman et al., 2019.

claim: The cell cycle duration of mESCs and NPCs is approximately twofold shorter than that of HCT116 cells.
source: Indeed, the cell cycle duration of mESCs and NPCs is approximately twofold shorter than that of HCT116 cells (Jensen et al., 2015; Waisman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Jensen et al., 2015 and Waisman et al., 2019.

claim: The Saos2 alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) cancer cell line requires SMC5/6 to promote telomere clustering and MiDAS at telomeres.
source: Another study reported that the Saos2 alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) cancer cell line requires SMC5/6 to promote telomere clustering and MiDAS at telomeres (Min et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Min et al., 2017.

claim: SMC5/6 has previously been shown to be critical for telomere clustering.
source: SMC5/6 has previously been shown to be critical for telomere clustering, and NSMCE2-mediated SUMOylation of shelterin components is important for ALT (Potts and Yu, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Potts and Yu, 2007.

claim: NSMCE2-mediated SUMOylation of shelterin components is important for ALT.
source: SMC5/6 has previously been shown to be critical for telomere clustering, and NSMCE2-mediated SUMOylation of shelterin components is important for ALT (Potts and Yu, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Potts and Yu, 2007.

claim: SMC5/6 localizes to pericentromeric heterochromatin, as revealed by previous work in mESCs, MEFs, and germ cells.
source: Notably, SMC5/6 localizes to pericentromeric heterochromatin, as revealed by our previous work in mESCs, MEFs, and germ cells, suggesting that it may play a direct role at these sites (Gómez et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016; Verver et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Gómez et al., 2013; Hwang et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2017; Pryzhkova and Jordan, 2016; and Verver et al., 2013.

claim: FANCD2 is highly expressed in mESCs.
source: It has been shown that FANCD2 is highly expressed in mESCs, though no comparison has been made with human cancer cells, and detailed studies of FANCD2 localization in mESCs have not been conducted (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: FA factors were recently shown to function upstream of SMC5/6 in the repair of exogenously induced inter-strand crosslinks (ICLs).
source: FA factors were recently shown to function upstream of SMC5/6 in the repair of exogenously induced inter-strand crosslinks (ICLs) (Rossi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Rossi et al., 2020.

claim: Deletion of RAD51 has been shown to rescue the lethality of SMC6 mutants in fission and budding yeast.
source: RAD51 can mediate the formation of toxic recombination intermediates, and deletion of RAD51 has been shown to rescue the lethality of SMC6 mutants in fission and budding yeast (Ampatzidou et al., 2006; Lehmann et al., 1995; Menolfi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Ampatzidou et al., 2006; Lehmann et al., 1995; and Menolfi et al., 2015.

claim: RAD51 foci are increased in Smc5 cKO MEFs following hydroxyurea treatment.
source: We previously showed that RAD51 foci are increased in Smc5 cKO MEFs following hydroxyurea treatment (Gaddipati et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to Gaddipati et al., 2019.

claim: SMC5/6 is necessary for the stabilization of stalled replication forks, rescue of collapsed replication forks, and repair of replication and recombination intermediates.
source: Together, these observations suggest that SMC5/6 is necessary for the stabilization of stalled replication forks, rescue of collapsed replication forks, and repair of replication and recombination intermediates.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Loss of SMC5/6 functions in the developing cortex leads to a reduction in cortex size, mislocalization of NPCs, reduced numbers of IPs and cortical layer neurons, and increased cell apoptosis.
source: We demonstrate that loss of SMC5/6 functions in the developing cortex leads to a reduction in cortex size, mislocalization of NPCs, reduced numbers of IPs and cortical layer neurons, and increased cell apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: SMC5/6 is required for proficient DNA replication, particularly at pericentromeric heterochromatin.
source: These developmental defects are attributed to SMC5/6 being required for proficient DNA replication, particularly at pericentromeric heterochromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: SMC5/6 depletion causes NPCs to enter mitosis with regions of under-replicated DNA, which results in chromosome segregation defects.
source: SMC5/6 depletion causes NPCs to enter mitosis with regions of under-replicated DNA, which results in chromosome segregation defects.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the main findings.

claim: Chromosome segregation defects stimulate a CHEK2-mediated DNA damage checkpoint response and result in elevated p53-mediated apoptosis.
source: These defects stimulate a CHEK2-mediated DNA damage checkpoint response and result in elevated p53-mediated apoptosis (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section and shown in Figure 7.
